payload.vignette:
A 2-year-old girl presented with skin fragility since early infancy. She had 2 older brothers, and the family had no medical history of note. Symptoms improved in winter and worsened in summer. Physical and mental developments were normal. The mother reported finding the child peeling off skin with marked facility.

Physical examination revealed:- Mild xerosis with superficial skin erosions- Erythematous residual macules from previous erosions- Some lesions had unusual linear geographic contour- Lesions predominantly located at areas of friction- Hair, nails, and mucous membranes were normal- No history of blistering

1. Laboratory Tests:- Serological markers for celiac disease were negative2. Skin Biopsy Findings:- Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed:  * Complete separation of the stratum corneum  * Clean split just above the stratum granulosum  * Faint psoriasiform hyperplasia  * Mild perivascular and interstitial mononuclear infiltrate in upper dermis3. Immunofluorescence Mapping:- Normal results for:  * Collagen IV and VII  * α6 and β4 integrines  * Laminine-3324. Genetic Study:- Revealed 2 heterozygous mutations in exon 2 of the CDSN geneImages:- Figure A Title: Clinical photograph of disease outbreak  Description: Superficial erosions distributed predominantly around the trunk, some with geometric shape- Figure B Title: Photograph showing localized affectation  Description: Erythemato-desquamative well-demarcated plaque with peeling borders on right foot- Figure C Title: Hematoxylin-eosin staining  Description: Detachment of entire stratum corneum and mild psoriasiform epidermis hyperplasia

payload.vignette:
A 2-year-old girl presented with skin fragility since early infancy. She had 2 older brothers, and the family had no medical history of note. Symptoms improved in winter and worsened in summer. Physical and mental developments were normal. The mother reported finding the child peeling off skin with marked facility.

Physical examination revealed:- Mild xerosis with superficial skin erosions- Erythematous residual macules from previous erosions- Some lesions had unusual linear geographic contour- Lesions predominantly located at areas of friction- Hair, nails, and mucous membranes were normal- No history of blistering

1. Laboratory Tests:- Serological markers for celiac disease were negative2. Skin Biopsy Findings:- Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed:  * Complete separation of the stratum corneum  * Clean split just above the stratum granulosum  * Faint psoriasiform hyperplasia  * Mild perivascular and interstitial mononuclear infiltrate in upper dermis3. Immunofluorescence Mapping:- Normal results for:  * Collagen IV and VII  * α6 and β4 integrines  * Laminine-3324. Genetic Study:- Revealed 2 heterozygous mutations in exon 2 of the CDSN geneImages:- Figure A Title: Clinical photograph of disease outbreak  Description: Superficial erosions distributed predominantly around the trunk, some with geometric shape- Figure B Title: Photograph showing localized affectation  Description: Erythemato-desquamative well-demarcated plaque with peeling borders on right foot- Figure C Title: Hematoxylin-eosin staining  Description: Detachment of entire stratum corneum and mild psoriasiform epidermis hyperplasia

payload.vignette:
A teenaged male presented with a 2-week history of vegetating, bleeding plaques and pustules on his face, scalp, trunk, and extremities. Lesions began as pustules and developed into painful, itchy plaques. Prior treatment included prednisolone tablet 5 mg twice daily, clindamycin hydrochloride 300 mg daily, and fluconazole 200 mg daily, but patient continued to develop new lesions. Patient reported difficulty walking due to skin lesions.

Pustules and hemorrhagic-crusted plaques were seen on the scalp, legs, arms, and trunk along with keloidal plaques on the face.

- Laboratory Tests:
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay testing for HIV was negative

- Histopathology:
Punch biopsy from arm showed:
- Epidermal hyperplasia and exocytosis of neutrophils
- Dense dermal-mixed inflammatory cell infiltration
- Microabscesses scattered with eosinophils
- No granulomas or multinucleated giant cells
- Negative periodic acid–Schiff staining

- Images:
Image A Title: Vegetative plaques on extremities
Description: Extensive vegetative plaques with bleeding and ulceration

Image B Title: Lesions on extremities and trunk
Description: Pustules and ulcerated plaques

Image C Title: Histopathologic examination (×100)
Description: Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (hematoxylin-eosin stain)

Image D Title: Histopathologic examination (×400)
Description: Dermal neutrophilia and microabscesses with eosinophilia (hematoxylin-eosin stain)

payload.vignette:
A woman in her 60s presented with an itchy plaque on the mid-back. She had had a lesion at that site since childhood, which had remained asymptomatic and pea sized for most of that time. However, over the 10 years prior to presentation it had gradually increased in size and became itchy. There was also occasional oozing of serosanguineous fluid and bleeding from the lesion.

Examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with overlying ulceration on the mid-back, 1 cm left of the spine. Adjoining skin showed a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.

- Histopathological examination:    - Revealed a circumscribed tumor contiguous with adjoining normal epidermis and delineated from underlying dermis by continuous apocrine epithelial lining    - Tumor epithelium with multiple papillary projections with vascular, plasma cell–rich stroma    - Several foci showed papillary projections lined by multilayered epithelium with atypical cells, few mitotic figures, and areas of necrosis but no dermal invasion      - Immunohistochemical analysis:    - p63 staining positive in myoepithelial cell layers    - Adjacent skin showed dermal papillae with congophilic amorphous eosinophilic deposits    - Pan-cytokeratin (AE1/3) immunostain positive  Images:  Figure 1 Title: Clinical Image of the Patient  Description: A 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with indented margin and overlying ulceration, located on the mid-back 1 cm left to the spine. Adjoining skin shows a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.  Figure 2 Title: Histopathologic Findings From Lesional Specimens  Description: Multiple microscopic images showing tumor architecture, cellular details, immunohistochemical staining, and dermal deposits.

payload.vignette:
A woman in her 60s presented with an itchy plaque on the mid-back. She had had a lesion at that site since childhood, which had remained asymptomatic and pea sized for most of that time. However, over the 10 years prior to presentation it had gradually increased in size and became itchy. There was also occasional oozing of serosanguineous fluid and bleeding from the lesion.

Examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with overlying ulceration on the mid-back, 1 cm left of the spine. Adjoining skin showed a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.

- Histopathological examination:    - Revealed a circumscribed tumor contiguous with adjoining normal epidermis and delineated from underlying dermis by continuous apocrine epithelial lining    - Tumor epithelium with multiple papillary projections with vascular, plasma cell–rich stroma    - Several foci showed papillary projections lined by multilayered epithelium with atypical cells, few mitotic figures, and areas of necrosis but no dermal invasion      - Immunohistochemical analysis:    - p63 staining positive in myoepithelial cell layers    - Adjacent skin showed dermal papillae with congophilic amorphous eosinophilic deposits    - Pan-cytokeratin (AE1/3) immunostain positive  Images:  Figure 1 Title: Clinical Image of the Patient  Description: A 1.5 × 1.0-cm well-defined erythematous plaque with indented margin and overlying ulceration, located on the mid-back 1 cm left to the spine. Adjoining skin shows a horseshoe-shaped oval area of lichenification.  Figure 2 Title: Histopathologic Findings From Lesional Specimens  Description: Multiple microscopic images showing tumor architecture, cellular details, immunohistochemical staining, and dermal deposits.

payload.vignette:
A woman in her 30s presented with asymptomatic erythematous scaly plaques over the face and proximal extremities. The lesions started as an erythematous papule on the face, progressing to larger plaques within 10 years. There was involvement of the upper respiratory tract, causing palatal perforation and stridor, necessitating a tracheostomy a year ago. History of wheezing and breathlessness. No history of preceding trauma, fever, malaise, joint pain, cough, epistaxis, hemoptysis, or hematuria.

Multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring measuring 2 × 1 to 8 × 7 cm on the face, arm, and thighs. Saddle nose deformity, perforation of the hard palate, and necrotic plaques on the ear with destruction of ear cartilage. Cervical lymphadenopathy: multiple, nontender, discrete nodes, ranging from 1.5 to 2 cm without surface changes. Sensory examination and peripheral nerve examination within normal limits. Respiratory examination normal.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Hemogram: anemia (hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL)
  - Kidney function test: normal
  - Liver function test: normal
  - Fasting blood glucose: normal
  - Urinalysis: normal

payload.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with a 12-year history of itchy eruptions over the whole body. Multiple nodules appeared on the upper back 1 year previously and gradually increased in number and size. The patient was otherwise healthy and denied a family history of inherited ichthyosis or atopy.

Physical examination revealed extensive, dry scaly patches on the trunk, arms, and legs. Several 0.5- to 1-cm, dome-shaped, red papules and nodules were found on the upper back. Mildly enlarged lymph nodes were observed on the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Routine blood tests, biochemistry analyses, and peripheral blood flow cytometry tests were within normal limits
  - No atypical cells were found in the peripheral blood
  - DNA analysis from paraffin sections showed clonal amplification product for the γ-chain of the T-cell receptor

- Histopathology:
  - Biopsy from back nodules showed:
    - Atrophy of the epidermis with focal orthokeratosis
    - Extensive, dense infiltrate of lymphocytes in the entire dermis
    - Small to medium-sized, atypical lymphocytes with focal areas of epidermotropism
  - Immunohistochemical staining showed:
    - Positive for CD2, CD3, CD4, and CD45RO
    - Few small reactive CD8+ T cells and CD7+ T cells in dermis

- Images:
  Title: Clinical and Histopathologic Images
  Description: Clinical images showing multiple dome-shaped nodules on the back and extensive, dry scaly patches on the leg. Histopathologic images showing small to medium-sized atypical cells, focal areas of epidermotropism, and CD4 on immunohistochemical analysis

payload.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with a 12-year history of itchy eruptions over the whole body. Multiple nodules appeared on the upper back 1 year previously and gradually increased in number and size. The patient was otherwise healthy and denied a family history of inherited ichthyosis or atopy.

Physical examination revealed extensive, dry scaly patches on the trunk, arms, and legs. Several 0.5- to 1-cm, dome-shaped, red papules and nodules were found on the upper back. Mildly enlarged lymph nodes were observed on the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Routine blood tests, biochemistry analyses, and peripheral blood flow cytometry tests were within normal limits
  - No atypical cells were found in the peripheral blood
  - DNA analysis from paraffin sections showed clonal amplification product for the γ-chain of the T-cell receptor

- Histopathology:
  - Biopsy from back nodules showed:
    - Atrophy of the epidermis with focal orthokeratosis
    - Extensive, dense infiltrate of lymphocytes in the entire dermis
    - Small to medium-sized, atypical lymphocytes with focal areas of epidermotropism
  - Immunohistochemical staining showed:
    - Positive for CD2, CD3, CD4, and CD45RO
    - Few small reactive CD8+ T cells and CD7+ T cells in dermis

- Images:
  Title: Clinical and Histopathologic Images
  Description: Clinical images showing multiple dome-shaped nodules on the back and extensive, dry scaly patches on the leg. Histopathologic images showing small to medium-sized atypical cells, focal areas of epidermotropism, and CD4 on immunohistochemical analysis

payload.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with new and progressive satellite lesions while undergoing pembrolizumab therapy. Two years earlier, he had undergone a wide local excision with graft repair for a left posterior auricular scalp lesion. An incidentally resected lymph node was found to be focally involved, with no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Within months, multiple unresectable satellite lesions appeared. He received 4 cycles of ipilimumab, followed by a second wide local excision when new lesions appeared. Additional satellite lesions developed and he began pembrolizumab therapy, but after 5 cycles, local progression occurred in the satellite lesions.

Multiple satellite lesions were present on the left posterior auricular scalp area. After treatment, clinically regressed lesions with persistent black pigmentation were noted.

- Histopathology:    Initial findings: Incidentally resected lymph node showed focal involvement        Post-treatment biopsy findings:    - H&E sections showed intense mixed superficial and deep dermal inflammatory infiltrate composed of numerous neutrophils, histiocytes, eosinophils, and lymphocytes    - Immunostaining results:      * SOX-10 and MART-1: Highlighted normal melanocytes in basal layer of epidermis only      * CD163 and myeloperoxidase: Highlighted histiocytes and neutrophils respectively        Images referenced:    Figure 1. Title: Recurrent Melanoma Lesions on the Left Posterior Auricular Scalp Before and After T-VEC Therapy    Figure 2. Title: Histopathologic Findings of T-VEC–Treated Melanoma Lesions    Description: Shows complete tumor regression and neutrophil-rich mixed inflammation; MART-1 immunostain confirms complete tumor regression

payload.vignette:
A man in his 40s with a medical history of factor VII deficiency hemophilia presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Following admission, he was intubated with prone positioning, and treatment was initiated. He was also found to have Staphylococcus hemolyticus bacteremia. Three days after admission, the patient developed erythema and edematous necrotic plaques of the bilateral ears. No devices had been used on the ears. The necrosis progressed during the following days, primarily involving the earlobe of the right ear and a large portion of the helix of the left ear.

Erythematous plaque (2 cm) with overlying eschar on the right earlobe. Multiple erythematous edematous erosions with eschar and crust on the helical rim of the left ear.

- Biopsy findings:    Image Title: Hematoxylin-eosin−stained biopsy specimens    Image Description: Detached epidermis with full-thickness necrosis overlying sparse inflammation associated with necrosis of adnexal epithelia, including folliculosebaceous units and eccrine glands. Epidermal and dermal necrosis and ulceration with necrosis of the eccrine glands.

payload.vignette:
A 75-year-old black woman with insulin-dependent diabetes and obesity presented with a 10-day history of pruritic lesions on her arms and legs, 2–3 months of night sweats, and 3 weeks of right-sided headache, sinus pain, and congestion. The skin lesions had developed while she was taking prednisone. She had no associated fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, myalgia, or arthralgia.

Patient looked well. On the extensor elbows extending down her forearms bilaterally and on her knees and shins were dozens of 1–2 cm oedematous pink-red papules with a darker red-violet central zone, resembling atypical papular target lesions. Along Wallace's lines on the medial aspect of her feet and the tips of her fingers and toes were about 20 red macules, 5–15 mm in diameter. She had one 2 mm erosion on the soft palate of her mouth; her face was otherwise spared.

Laboratory Tests:
- White blood cell count 2.7 × 10⁹/L (43% neutrophils, 37% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, 1% atypical lymphocytes, 10% bands)
- Haemoglobin: 100 g/L
- Platelet count: 129 × 10⁹/L
- Absolute neutrophil count 1.4 × 10⁹/L
- Normal liver function tests
- Urinalysis: 2+ protein, no blood
- Negative PCR for herpes simplex virus, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and cryoglobulins
- Antinuclear antibody: <1:40
- Elevated IgA: 8860 mg/L (normal range: 700–4000 mg/L)

Skin Biopsy:
- Infiltrate of atypical mononuclear cells around vessels
- Vascular damage with extravasated erythrocytes, leucocytoclasia, and fibrinoid degeneration
- Atypical cells positive for myeloperoxidase, CD15, CD43, CD45, CD68, TIA-1

Bone Marrow Biopsy:
- 5% CD34+ myeloblasts
- Abnormal localisation of immature precursors
- Dysmegakaryopoiesis in normocellular marrow

Cytogenetics:
- Complex karyotype with chromosomal abnormalities
- FISH showed deletions of 5q and 7q in 54% of bone marrow cells

Imaging:
Figure 1 - Title: Skin lesions and biopsy findings
Description: (A) Oedematous red papules and plaques with darker central zone on right arm. (B) Skin biopsy showing vessel wall infiltration by atypical mononuclear cells with fibrin deposition.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

No exacerbating or alleviating factors were noted. She was a nonsmoker and did not report recreational drugs or alcohol. Family history notable for father with renal cell carcinoma. Medical history included hypertension, basal cell carcinoma in remission, and an autoimmune condition diagnosed 16 years ago. Patient had been on long-term azathioprine therapy (125 mg daily, later reduced to 100 mg daily) and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. Four years after initial diagnosis, she experienced unintentional weight loss, fever, polyarthralgia, and fatigue.

Patient was hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed tenderness at the left costovertebral angle.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Hemoglobin: 114 g/L (Normal: 125-165)    * WBC: 6.17 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 4-10.8)    * ANC: 2.75 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 1.5-7.8)    * ALC: 3.32 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 0.85-3.9)    * AMC: 1.15 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 0.299-0.95)    * AEC: 0.12 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 0.02-0.5)    * LDH: 3.03 µkat/L (Normal: 2.33-4.67)    * Creatinine: 95.47 µmol/L (Normal: 53.04-97.24)    * ESR: 54 mm/hr (Normal: 0-20)    * CRP: 6.1 mg/L (Normal: <8)  - Imaging Studies:    * CT Scan Title: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen    * CT Scan Description: 7 cm × 5 cm × 5 cm heterogenous left adrenal mass containing regions of necrosis, with local extension into and invasion of the pancreatic tail, left hemidiaphragm, and spleen, along with the presence of multiple enlarged regional lymph nodes.

- Bilateral pleural effusion with oxygen saturation at 87%
- Grade 2 ascites with shifting dullness and fluid wave
- Hardened and hyperpigmented skin on the limbs
- Arthritis in the hands with ulnar deviation of the wrists
- Lower-limb edema
- Muscle strength of 4/5

- Hemoglobin: 13 g/dL
- Leukocytes: 6.4 (1000/mm³)
- Lymphocytes: 1.38 (1000/mm³)
- C-reactive protein: 4.4 mg/L (elevated)
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 37 mm/hr (elevated)
- Albumin: 1.7 g/dL (low)
- Complement C3: 36.9 mg/dL (low)
- Anti-Sm antibody: 36.22 U (weak positive)
- Antinuclear antibodies: Fine speckled 4+, mitochondrial 3+

Imaging and Other Tests:
- Capillaroscopy Image Description: Late signs with avascular areas
- Computed Tomography: Showed interstitial lung disease
- Echocardiography: Intermediate probability of pulmonary hypertension
- Spirometry: Findings suggestive of pulmonary restriction
- Schirmer test: Showed significant decrease in tear secretion
- Skin biopsies: Increased collagen and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate

Ascitic Fluid Analysis:
- High albumin gradient initially
- Abundant leukocytes, predominantly lymphocytes
- Reactive mesothelial cells
- Negative cytology for malignancy
- Negative cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria

payload.vignette:
A 56-year-old woman with locally advanced, unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma. She initially received four cycles of Folfirinox chemotherapy without significant response, followed by gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel therapy. After 20 cycles of combined therapy and 16 additional cycles of nab-paclitaxel alone, she developed bilateral facial drooping, inability to close her eyelids, and difficulty raising her eyebrows. Prior to this, she had experienced grade 1 peripheral neuropathy which remained stable while taking vitamin B6 supplements, and had developed severe edema due to capillary leak which led to discontinuation of gemcitabine.

Neurological evaluation revealed bilateral lower motor neuron facial muscle weakness.

Medical history included dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peripheral artery disease, and coronary artery disease with previous percutaneous coronary intervention to the left anterior descending and right coronary artery.

Patient was febrile (Tmax 39.3°C [102.8 °F]), hypoxic with SpO₂ of 88% on room air, blood pressure of 125/62 mm Hg, heart rate of 98 beats/min, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min.

- Laboratory findings:    - Leukocyte count: 13.4 × 10⁹/L (normal: 4.1–11.1 × 10⁹/L)    - Sodium: 129 mmol/L (normal: 135–146 mmol/L)    - High-sensitivity troponin: 102 μg/L (normal: <78 μg/L)    - N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide: 1098 ng/L (normal: 0–900 ng/L)    - Positive Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 antigen in urine    - Negative SARS-CoV-2 and influenza tests  - Imaging Studies:    - Chest radiograph: Right-sided lung infiltrates    - ECG findings (Figure 1): Sinus tachycardia with old incomplete right bundle branch block, new left posterior fascicular block, multifocal PVCs, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, fascicular ventricular tachycardia    - Echocardiography: LVEF 50%, no regional wall motion or valvular abnormalities    - Coronary angiography: Stable findings, no significant changes from previous    - Cardiac MRI findings (Figure 2):      - LVEF 46%      - Moderate subendocardial LGE in multiple segments      - Subepicardial LGE in apical inferior wall and papillary muscles    - 18F-FDG-PET/CT findings (Figure 3):      - LVEF 59%      - Perfusion defects in basal-mid-inferior/inferoseptal and mid-anteroseptal walls      - FDG uptake in posteromedial papillary muscle and anterolateral wall

payload.vignette:
A 76-year-old man with numerous cardiovascular comorbid conditions presented with weeks of worsening renal function leading to hospitalization. Home medications included rosuvastatin, aspirin, prasugrel, sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, ezetimibe, furosemide, and ferrous sulfate. Several weeks after starting a new medication, he experienced decreased appetite, weakness, and fatigue, which persisted for several months. The medication was discontinued after approximately 3.5 months of treatment (two weeks before hospitalization). Despite discontinuation, he still experienced poor appetite and profound weakness, needing a wheelchair. He had one fall approximately one week before presentation, during which he was briefly immobilized.

Patient required wheelchair for mobility. No evidence of physical trauma or findings concerning for compartment syndrome was noted. Subsequently developed reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, oliguria, and rapid atrial fibrillation.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Serum creatinine increased to 760.24 µmol/L (8.61 mg/dL)    * Creatine kinase level: 10,698 U/L    * Urinalysis showed myoglobinuria    * Urine sediment showed acute tubular necrosis with muddy brown casts    * Additional findings: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, lactic acid increased to 10 mmol/L      - Other Tests:    * ANA: Negative    * Tickborne panel: Negative      - Imaging:    * CT abdomen and pelvis showed no hydronephrosis      Figure Title: Serum creatinine relative to medication initiation/discontinuation

payload.vignette:
A 45-year-old Filipino woman presented with a 2-day history of right-sided headache and emesis of clear fluid. She reported dizziness and generalized weakness but did not report chills, rigor, neck pain, unilateral limb weakness, or sensory loss. No pulmonary, gastrointestinal, or urinary symptoms were present. Medical history included right tympanomastoidectomy for cholesteatoma 2 months prior.

Patient was acutely ill with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. She was afebrile and normotensive, with normal strength in all four extremities. Cranial nerves were intact. Right mastoid region showed a small gaping mastoidectomy wound with a small amount of greenish discharge. Otoscopy revealed greenish discharge in the right external auditory canal. Tympanic membrane was intact. Funduscopy showed no papilledema.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Leukocyte count: 7.1 × 10⁹/L    * C-reactive protein level: 500 mg/L (normal: <1.5 mg/L)- Imaging Studies:    * Computed Tomography with contrast    Image Title: Contrast computed tomography of brain    Image Description: Right temporal lobe ring-enhancing lesion measuring 5.7 cm × 4.8 cm × 5.2 cm with a gas-fluid level and gas bubbles. Significant leftward midline shift with subfalcine and left transtentorial herniation.- Microbiology:    * Cultures revealed Proteus mirabilis and Enterococcus gallinarum    * Fungal, Nocardia, and Actinomyces cultures were negative

A 78-year-old man with a history of liver cirrhosis due to primary biliary cholangitis and curative treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia. He was admitted during regular hospital check-ups due to unstable vital signs.

- Blood pressure: 70/40 mm Hg- Heart rate: 50/min- SpO₂: 92% (room air)- Temperature: 37.8°C- Reduced breath sounds in the right lower lung- Jaundice in eyes

Laboratory Tests:- Leukocyte count: 28.11 × 10⁹/L- C-reactive protein level: 119.90 mg/L- Procalcitonin concentration: 3.90 µg/L- Complete blood count and chemistry details as per Table 1, showing abnormal coagulation findings- Cultures of lung fluid and blood were positiveImaging Studies:- Image Title: Computed tomography scan (Figure 1A)- Image Description: Massive pleural effusion in the right lower lung lobe- Image Title: Follow-up computed tomography scan (Figure 1B)- Image Description: Shows disappearance of the massive empyema after treatment

  Image Description: Showed soft tissue calcifications unrelated to bone or cartilage, negative for osteomyelitis or subcutaneous gas
- CT scan of right lower extremity
  Image Description: Sagittal view at the level of the cuboid and fibular malleolus showing soft tissue calcifications

Pathology:
- Findings confirmed calcified tissue with inflamed stroma and necrosis

Patient was tachycardic, diaphoretic, and febrile. Several areas of skin over his face, chest, and abdomen showed hardened plaque and depigmentation. Over the upper extremities, hardened nodules of varying sizes were noted, along with larger hardened masses that were fixed and nontender to palpation. The right foot/ankle was fluctuant and tender to palpation.

Laboratory Results:
- Normal renal function
- Leukocytosis (WBC count: 18.7 × 10³/UL)
- Elevated total creatine kinase (1947 U/L)
- Normal corrected calcium (9.62 mg/dL)
- Depressed phosphorus (1.7 mg/dL)
- Normal lactic acid (1.7 mmol/L) and magnesium (1.9 mg/dL)

Imaging Studies:
- X-ray sagittal view of right lower extremity
  Image Description: Showed soft tissue calcifications unrelated to bone or cartilage, negative for osteomyelitis or subcutaneous gas
- CT scan of right lower extremity
  Image Description: Sagittal view at the level of the cuboid and fibular malleolus showing soft tissue calcifications

Pathology:
- Findings confirmed calcified tissue with inflamed stroma and necrosis

The patient did not report shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, lower extremity weakness, or abdominal, back, or chest pain. A previous scan 9 years prior showed the mass was 3 cm.

Vital signs: Temperature - afebrile, Blood pressure - 120/76 mm Hg, Pulse rate - 73 beats/min, Respiratory rate - 16/minute. Examination revealed a well-defined large pulsatile mass palpable in the epigastric region with a soft bruit audible on auscultation. Pulses were palpable in the lower extremities bilaterally.

- Laboratory tests: Complete blood count and electrolyte levels were within normal limits.

- Imaging Studies:
  1. Computed tomographic angiogram (CTA) of abdomen and pelvis:
    Image Title: Figure 1 - CTA Abdomen and Pelvis
    Image Description: (A) Axial view showing a saccular aneurysm measuring 14.6 cm × 12.6 cm in greatest transaxial dimension. (B) Sagittal view showing 14.7 cm craniocaudal dimension. The right ureter was significantly displaced anterolaterally. Dense calcifications of iliac vessels present without narrowing. No signs of impending rupture. Aneurysmal neck angulation greater than 60 degrees with neck tortuosity noted.

A 64-year-old White woman with epilepsy and osteoporosis presented with a 10-day history of worsening, intermittent epigastric pain, distention, and constipation. Pain was nonradiating and cramping. Family history included ulcerative colitis in her mother. Prior endoscopic work-up included two screening colonoscopies (as recent as five months prior), but no upper endoscopy.

Patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness with mild distention.

  * Liver function tests: normal
  * Lipase: 10 U/L (upper limit of normal, 81 U/L)

    Title: Initial CT abdomen and pelvis
    Description: Revealed duodenal diverticula, wall thickening with mesenteric edema approximately 25 cm beyond the ligament of Treitz, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with luminal patency

  * Follow-up CT scan (one month later):
    Title: Follow-up CT abdomen and pelvis
    Description: Showed resolution of inflammatory changes

- Endoscopic studies:
  * Capsule endoscopy performed but images of the diverticula were not captured

Other Tests:

A 56-year-old female with medical history of type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and nonischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 25% to 34%). Patient was afebrile and hemodynamically stable with 98% oxygen saturation on room air. payload.vignette:
A 45-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of left-sided pyelonephritis. Medical history included 9 spontaneous abortions and one completed pregnancy, with previous workup negative for antiphospholipid syndrome and protein C deficiency. No personal or family history of clotting or liver disease. Patient was a lifetime nonsmoker, seldom drank alcohol, and was not taking any medications or supplements.

Patient was febrile at triage but hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed diaphoresis and left flank pain. No right-upper-quadrant tenderness or hepatomegaly was noted.

- Laboratory findings: Initially elevated international normalized ratio of 1.4 (resolved to 1.0 within 3 days), activated prothrombin time 29.3s (normal range 28.0-38.0s). Other hepatic function tests and standard investigations were unremarkable.- Imaging Studies:  1. Abdominal CT scan:     - Cortical enhancement of left kidney with surrounding inflammatory stranding     - Multifocal peripheral dilation of bile ducts at right liver lobe     - Relative atrophy of left lobe     - Liver showed smooth contours with no signs of cirrhosis    2. MRI:     Image Title: Arterial-phase fat-saturated T1-weighted magnetic resonance image     Image Description: Demonstrates a 2.8-cm filling defect in the common hepatic artery

She had lingual and palatal dysarthria, and slow, but symmetric palate elevation. The rest of her neurological exam, including muscle and facial strength and reflexes, was unremarkable.

Infiltration of the intrinsic tongue muscles with tongue atrophy.    3. Flexible laryngoscopy: Shows base of tongue fullness with prominent lymphatic tissue  - Pathology:  Biopsy results: Focal, non-keratinizing invasive squamous cell carcinoma  Additional findings: P16– INK and Cyto5/6 immunohistochemistry were positive

A 2-year-old girl was admitted with 2-day history of fever, severe sore throat, neck pain, vomiting and poor intake. She looked fatigue with moderate dehydration. She had no significant past medical history.

Laboratory Tests:- Hemoglobin: 12.9 g/dL- Leukocyte count: 10,170 cells/mm3 (lymphocyte 51%, neutrophil 41%, monocyte 8%)- Platelet count: 239,000 cells/mm3- ESR: 6 mm/hr- Procalcitonin: 0.20 ng/mL- Normal liver transaminases- CSF analysis: leukocyte 250 cells/mm3 (neutrophil 20%, lymphocyte 80%), glucose 58 mg/dL, protein 35 mg/dLSerology:- Positive viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM- Negative VCA IgG- Absent Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen (EBNA)- Positive EBV DNA in CSFImaging Studies:- CT head/neck findings: Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement along bilateral parietal cortical sulci and around brainstem, small hypodense lesion in left high parietal lobe, bilateral tonsillitis and multiple cervical lymphadenopathies- MRI findings: Regression of leptomeningeal enhancement along brainstem surface, circumferential T2/FLAIR hyperintense rim at midbrain and pons, subacute cortical infarction at parasagittal bilateral parietal lobes, thin subdural hemorrhage along left temporooccipital convexities

Laboratory Tests:- CRP: 14 mg/L (mildly elevated)- White blood cell count: 6.2 × 10^9/L- Absolute lymphocyte count: 1.42 × 10^9/L (23% of total white blood cells)Imaging Studies:1. Initial Chest CT (March 10th, 2022)- Description: Ground glass opacities and 'crazy paving' pattern bilaterally in the lower lobes2. Second Chest X-ray (April 26th, 2022)- Description: Bilateral ground-glass appearance with progression in haziness in both lower and middle lung fields4. Follow-up Chest X-ray (May 14th, 2022)- Description: Improvement in bilateral infiltrationsOther Tests:- RT-PCR test of sputum: Positive for SARS-CoV-2- COVID-19 antibody test: Initially negative (remained negative for approximately 40 days after first positive PCR)

payload.vignette:
A 39-year-old female teacher from Southwest China presented with a subcutaneous mass in the lower-left abdominal region. The patient had a history of chronic urticaria (relieved by occasional use of loratadine), cesarean section eight years ago, and myomectomy to remove a myoma six months ago. She denied a history of dysmenorrhea and abortion. The mass was accompanied by slight pain that worsened around menstruation.

Heart, lungs, and abdomen showed no obvious abnormalities. No palpable swelling of superficial lymph nodes was noted. A subcutaneous nodule of approximately 1 cm diameter was present under the hypogastrium. The nodule's surface was normal, without ulceration or bleeding. A linear scar was observed in the lower-left abdominal region.

payload.vignette:
A 66-year-old female patient with a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and thrombocytopenia. The patient had consistently shown leukocytopenia and thrombocytopenia in routine blood tests over the years. Initial blood test revealed a leukocyte count of 3.16 × 10^9/L and a platelet count of 109.00 × 10^9/L. No other symptoms were present, and no significant abnormalities were detected in cardiac enzymes or blood coagulation. Four hours post-procedure, the patient experienced intermittent abdominal pain and occasional nausea. Nine hours following the operation, the patient experienced recurrent right abdomen pain progressing to involve the entire abdomen, with persistent nausea and perceived increase in body temperature.

Initial examination showed tenderness in the right abdomen, without rebound tenderness and muscular tension, with normal bowel sounds. Later examination revealed diffuse tenderness with rebound tenderness, primarily in the right abdomen. Dullness to percussion was observed, while pain during percussion in the liver area was absent. Shifting dullness to percussion was negative, and normal bowel sounds were detected. Maximum body temperature was 37.8°C.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - WBC count: 3.43 × 10^9/L
  - Neutrophil percentage: 85.40%
  - Lymphocyte percentage: 9.40%
  - Absolute lymphocytes: 0.32 × 10^9/L
  - Platelet count: 79.00 × 10^9/L
  - CRP level: 2.45 mg/L
  - Procalcitonin level: 0.58 ng/ml

- Imaging Studies:
  CT Scan Results: Edematous thickening of the intestinal wall in the ascending colon with peripheral exudative changes. No signs of intestinal perforation or obstruction.
  Follow-up CT: Distension of anterior wall of ascending colon with gas, exudation in subserosa of middle section, and small quantity of ascites.

- Bacterial Culture:
  Ascites culture yielded growth of Escherichia coli.

- Histological Examination:
  Showed edema in all layers of intestinal wall, predominant thickening and edema in submucosa, diffuse infiltration of neutrophils with presence of abscesses. Bacterial colonies observed in submucosa surrounding the ESD lesion.

payload.vignette:
A full-term girl presented at birth with multiple skin lesions. One month later, she returned due to recurring skin eruptions. She was born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. Growth and development were normal for her age and sex. The patient's family medical history was unremarkable. At 3-year follow-up, the vesicles and bullae began decreasing at 6 months old but intermittently returned after 1 year of age.

Initial exam: Multiple areas of erythema, vesicles, and bullae on the face, trunk, and extremities. Vital signs including temperature, respiration, and heart rate were within normal ranges. Follow-up exam: Multiple round or irregularly shaped erythematous macules and slightly scaly plaques of various sizes on face, trunk, and extremities. Bullous and vesicular lesions on thighs, with scattered facial erosions. Mucous membranes not affected. Later developed thickened, brown, corrugated plaques over neck, armpits, wrists, and ankles, along with palmoplantar hyperkeratosis.

- Skin-punch biopsy: Revealed hyperkeratosis, distinct vacuolization in the granular and upper spinous layers, and bullae formation within the epidermis, with sparse inflammatory cells in the superficial dermis.- Direct immunofluorescence (DIF): Results were unremarkable.- Genetic testing: Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous variation c.482T>C (p. L161P) in KRT1.- Images:  Figure 1A Title: Hyperkeratotic plaques  Figure 1A Description: Hyperkeratotic plaques with distinct borders and annular appearance    Figure 1B Title: Histopathology of erythematous scaly plaque  Figure 1B Description: Shows hyperkeratosis, spinous cell vacuolization, and vesicles in the epidermis    Figure 2 Title: Histopathological examination  Figure 2 Description: Hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100

payload.vignette:
A man in his 60s with systemic sclerosis presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Past medical history included heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon. He was receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily. The patient's other medical history was unremarkable.

Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas.

- Laboratory Tests:
  Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable.

- Pathology:
  Lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with one additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array.
  Tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus.

- Clinical Images:
  Image A Title: Clinical image of proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk
  Image A Description: Firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale

  Image B Title: Clinical image of right shoulder and chest
  Image B Description: Nodular plaques

  Images C and D Title: Lesional punch biopsy specimens
  Images C and D Description: Hematoxylin-eosin stained specimens

payload.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.

- Histopathologic examination:    Image A: Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion    Image B: Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex    Image C: Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)    Image D: High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)  - Laboratory findings:    - Direct immunofluorescence: Positive with granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels    - Antinuclear antibody: Negative    - Antidouble-stranded DNA antibody: Negative    - All other laboratory test findings were normal

payload.vignette:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.

- Histopathologic examination:    Image A: Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion    Image B: Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex    Image C: Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)    Image D: High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)  - Laboratory findings:    - Direct immunofluorescence: Positive with granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels    - Antinuclear antibody: Negative    - Antidouble-stranded DNA antibody: Negative    - All other laboratory test findings were normal

Each paced QRS complex is followed by a premature ventricular complex (PVC), with a second pacemaker stimulus occurring about 60 msec after onset of the PVC.        Image Title: Figure 1. payload.vignette:
A woman in her 50s with a history of chronic pulmonary coccidiomycosis being treated with fluconazole was admitted for fever, hypotension, and rash. Three months prior, pembrolizumab treatment was stopped because of a widespread morbilliform reaction, which had resolved completely 6 to 8 weeks before admission. The new widespread, asymptomatic skin eruption had been ongoing for 1 to 2 weeks and appeared different from her previous reaction.

Total body skin examination findings were notable for widespread, nontender, erythematous patches and thin plaques, some with prominent overlying telangiectases and hyperpigmentation.

- Laboratory tests: Complete blood cell count showed white blood cell count of 4100/μL, absolute neutrophil count of 2940/μL, hemoglobin level of 8.2 g/dL, and platelet count of 62 ×103/μL. Blood culture results showed no growth at 1 week. Serum β-D-glucan, galactomannan, Coccidioides antibody by complement fixation, and immunodiffusion results were negative. Respiratory viral panel and SARS-CoV-2 test results were negative.- Pathology:   Image Title: Skin Biopsy Findings  Image Description: Hematoxylin-eosin stained sections and CD56 immunostaining showing intravascular atypical cells.- Additional Tests:  - Brain MRI performed  - Lumbar puncture performed  - Bone marrow biopsy performed

payload.vignette:
A Chinese woman in her late 20s presented with a 20-year history of progressive skin laxity. In early childhood, she had developed asymptomatic yellowish coalesced papules confined to flexural areas. Subsequently, severe skin sagging occurred on her abdomen with loss of elasticity, then spread extensively with developmental growth. The patient had no extracutaneous involvement and was born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents. Her younger sister had developed the same skin symptoms.

Thick and leathery skinfolds on the neck, axillae, inguinal regions, abdomen, and limbs, with yellowish papules scattered on the dorsal neck.

- Laboratory tests:     - Low clotting activity of factor X (52.2%; reference range, 77%-131%)    - Prolonged prothrombin time (12.8 seconds; reference range, 10.4-12.6 seconds)    - Other laboratory investigations were unremarkable      - Imaging studies:    - Echocardiographic examination results were normal    - Fundoscopic examination results were normal  - Histopathology:    Image Title: Skin biopsy specimen from neck    Image Description: Shows excessive calcification of elastic fiber fragments scattered in the reticular dermis (von Kossa staining)  - Genetic Testing:    Whole-exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous sequence variation in GGCX gene:    - c.1167_1172delCTGGACinsGGGAA (p. Asn389Lys fs*13) in exon 8     - c.824C>T (p. Ser275Leu) in exon 7

payload.vignette:
A young black woman presented with painful lesions on both legs. She reported chills, bilateral lower extremity swelling, and several small, painful, 'pimple-like bumps' appearing on her bilateral lower legs, which ulcerated several days later. The ulcers progressed despite a recent course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for cultures growing methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Medical history includes treatment with methimazole and atenolol for the past year. No other medications or supplements were reported.

Bilateral lower extremities revealed pitting edema and multiple discrete, round, dry ulcers, most with central eschars, dusky gray borders, and collarettes of scale. During follow-up, an intact 4-mm papular lesion was identified on her lower right leg. No pathergy at the previous punch biopsy site was observed.

- Laboratory tests:     - Elevated C-reactive protein     - Increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate    - Normal C3 and C4 complement levels    - ANA titer 1:80 (reference range, <1:40)    - P-ANCA titer 1:20 (reference range, <1:20)    - Anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) titer 141 U (reference range, <2.8 U)    - Anti-SSA/Ro antibodies level 120 U (reference range, 0-40 U)  - Pathology:    - Initial punch biopsy: Mid- and deep dermal marked lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with neutrophils and focal abscess    - Second biopsy of intact papule: Intraepidermal and dermal perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate with marked papillary dermal edema, necrosis of vessel walls, and focal fibrinoid necrosis    - Special stains (PAS-diastase, GMS, Brown-Brenn, AFB): Negative for organisms  - Images:    Image A: Discrete, round, dry ulcers with central eschar and raised borders on left lateral lower leg    Image B: A new, 4-mm intact papule on right medial lower leg    Images C and D: Histopathological images from punch biopsy specimen of the papule, hematoxylin-eosin

payload.vignette:
A 78-year-old man presented with painful swelling and ulceration of the glans penis of 1 month's duration. His medical history included an elevated white blood cell count and inguinal lymphadenopathy discovered 9 years prior. Four years after initial presentation, he experienced fatigue, weight loss, and loss of appetite. The current illness began 1 month prior to admission when he noticed asymptomatic 'green-yellow welts' and swelling of the glans penis. The swelling became progressively painful and evolved to the size of an 'orange' over 4 days. Previous treatments with topical antibiotics, antifungal agents, hydrogen peroxide soaks, warm compresses, and cephalexin showed no improvement.

Patient appeared healthy. The glans penis and corona were grossly edematous, with a 3.7 × 3.3-cm tender, firm ulcer on the ventral surface of the penis with overlying black eschar, adherent yellow crust, and granulation tissue. No urethral discharge was present.

- Laboratory Tests: Routine blood test results were within normal limits. Cultures, assays, and blood tests evaluating for viral, bacterial, or fungal etiology were negative.

- Pathology Studies: Biopsy of the glans penis ulcer showed dermal infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes, which were CD20+, CD79a+, and CD5+, within the background of a reactive T-cell infiltrate. PCR analysis revealed a clonal IgH gene rearrangement.

- Imaging Studies: PET-CT scan demonstrated FDG-avid abdominal and peripancreatic lymph nodes.

- Imaging Studies: PET-CT scan demonstrated FDG-avid abdominal and peripancreatic lymph nodes.

A 31-year-old male nursing student with a history of axillary hyperhidrosis presented with excessive sweating of the buttocks, most severe at the intergluteal cleft and sacrum. He had previously treated his axillary condition successfully with 20% aluminum chloride; however, treatment of the intergluteal cleft and sacrum with aluminum chloride was unsuccessful. Due to the severity of the condition, he used absorbent pads yet continued to soak through his pants and was consequently unable to attend work.

The Minor starch-iodine test was performed to help localize the sites of overactive sweating. Areas of significant sweating were identified in the sacral region (10 × 3-cm area) and intergluteal cleft (6 × 8-cm area).

payload.vignette:
A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears. Similar vesicles were observed at the upper and lower vermillion border. Several erythematous papules and crusts were located on the cheeks, neck, and lower arms.

- Laboratory tests: Differential blood count, routine chemical analysis, and serum porphyrins were unremarkable. Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable. Bacterial cultures from blister fluid were unremarkable.- Virologic analyses: Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses. PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

payload.vignette:
A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears. Similar vesicles were observed at the upper and lower vermillion border. Several erythematous papules and crusts were located on the cheeks, neck, and lower arms.

- Laboratory tests: Differential blood count, routine chemical analysis, and serum porphyrins were unremarkable. Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable. Bacterial cultures from blister fluid were unremarkable.- Virologic analyses: Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses. PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

payload.vignette:
A female patient in her early 50s presented with multiple (approximately 10) bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. The lesions had been growing very slowly in number and size since age 24 and had been bleeding occasionally after trauma. The patient used a wheelchair due to right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia caused by an intracranial hemorrhage. At age 4, she had recurrent seizures. She had lipolymphedema of the lower legs attributed to functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity, and had been wearing compression stockings for years. Family history revealed similar conditions in the patient's father and aunt, with the father having died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s.

Multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. Lipolymphedema of the lower legs was present. Right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia were noted.

- Sonography: Demonstrated intradermal slow-flow vascular malformations with a maximum diameter of 1.2 cm.

- Histopathology:
  Image Description: Biopsy revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis of the epidermis overlying a conglomerate of dilated venous-like malformations with continuous smooth muscle in the upper dermis, partly showing thrombosis.

- Genetic Testing:
  Result: Detection of a heterozygous pathogenic KRIT1 variant.

Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. payload.vignette:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

- Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):  Image Title: OCT Scans  Image Description: Right eye showed significant cystoid macular edema and subfoveal fluid. Left eye had a mild epiretinal membrane.- Fluorescein Angiography:  Image Title: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography  Image Description: Revealed cystoid macular edema with leakage in both right and left eyes.- Blood Tests: Tests for vasculitis and rheumatologic disorders were within reference limits. Normal findings for tick-borne and bacterial diseases.- Imaging:  Computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable.

payload.vignette:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

Because of his headache, an MRI of the brain was obtained, which demonstrated vasogenic edema in the left posterior insula and temporoparietal cortex, intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the same region, and overlying leptomeningeal enhancement—findings consistent with hemorrhagic meningoencephalitis.

payload.vignette:
A 41-year-old woman with a 3-month history of sacroiliac pain, arthralgias, and lower-limb myalgias partially responsive to NSAIDs was diagnosed with seronegative spondyloarthropathy (negative HLA-B27) after MRI confirmed bilateral active sacroiliitis. Two months later, she began weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg with significant improvement in her joint symptoms. After the third dose, she developed a dry cough and dyspnea on moderate exertion without fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. She denied tobacco use, recent travel, or exposures to animals, dusts, or sick contacts. 

On examination in the emergency department, she was afebrile, blood pressure 118/84 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygenation normal on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed scant basal “Velcro”-like crackles. Other exams were unremarkable apart from positive sacroiliac provocation tests. 

Laboratory studies: Hb 13 g/dL, WBC 4,100/mm³ (neutrophils 2,000, lymphocytes 1,400), eosinophils 50/mm³, platelets 325,000/mm³; AST, ALT, bilirubin, creatinine, and BUN were within normal limits. 

High-resolution chest CT showed ground-glass interstitial infiltrates with a centrifugal distribution, predominantly in the upper lobes, and a mosaic pattern of disseminated attenuation without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. An echocardiogram was normal, and ECG showed sinus rhythm. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed no endobronchial lesions; GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and methenamine silver stain were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 41-year-old woman with a 3-month history of sacroiliac pain, arthralgias, and lower-limb myalgias partially responsive to NSAIDs was diagnosed with seronegative spondyloarthropathy (negative HLA-B27) after MRI confirmed bilateral active sacroiliitis. Two months later, she began weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg with significant improvement in her joint symptoms. After the third dose, she developed a dry cough and dyspnea on moderate exertion without fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. She denied tobacco use, recent travel, or exposures to animals, dusts, or sick contacts. 

On examination in the emergency department, she was afebrile, blood pressure 118/84 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygenation normal on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed scant basal “Velcro”-like crackles. Other exams were unremarkable apart from positive sacroiliac provocation tests.

High-resolution chest CT showed ground-glass interstitial infiltrates with a centrifugal distribution, predominantly in the upper lobes, and a mosaic pattern of disseminated attenuation without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. An echocardiogram was normal, and ECG showed sinus rhythm. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed no endobronchial lesions; GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and methenamine silver stain were negative.

payload.vignette:
• A 74-year-old man was referred after an antero-septal STEMI treated with primary PCI and stenting from the left main to the LAD.  
• Past history: dyslipidemia, overweight (BMI 25.8 kg/m²), active smoker, surgically repaired infra-renal abdominal aortic aneurysm.  
• Physical exam: unremarkable cardiovascular and respiratory findings.  
• Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE): mild LV dilation (EDD 57 mm), LVEF 46% due to anterior/mid-septal and apical akinesia; grade II diastolic dysfunction; severe LA enlargement; sclerotic aortic and mitral leaflets with mild AR and moderate MR; normal RV size and function; mild TR (PASP 52 mmHg); normal IVC; no pericardial effusion; mild ascending aorta dilation.  
• TTE also identified a ~9 mm round, hyperechoic mass adherent to the ventricular surface of the anterior tricuspid leaflet, moving toward the RA in systole.  
• Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed a 6×8 mm non-solid structure on the ventricular aspect of the anterior tricuspid leaflet with a “finger-in-glove” blind-ended protrusion, internally empty with filamentous adherent elements (“garland-like”), echogenicity matching adjacent tissue, bulging in systole and relaxing in diastole.  
• The patient remained asymptomatic. Contrast-enhanced chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism, and blood cultures were negative.

• The patient remained asymptomatic. Contrast-enhanced chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism, and blood cultures were negative.

payload.vignette:
A 30-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-week history of worsening crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and bloody diarrhea. She denied smoking or alcohol use. Her only medication was a progesterone-only contraceptive, which she had been taking for 2 months.

On examination, her temperature was normal, blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 114 bpm, and BMI 32.3. Abdominal palpation revealed diffuse tenderness without guarding or rigidity; bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation studies; C-reactive protein was 4.8 mg/dL. Stool cultures and assays for Clostridioides difficile toxins were negative. Fecal calprotectin was elevated at 2006 µg/g (reference 10–50 µg/g).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated mild thickening of the mid- and distal descending colon with adjacent inflammatory stranding; there was no evidence of perforation, abscess, or diverticulosis.

She was treated with intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and pain medications, and received a single dose of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. 

Colonoscopy revealed segmental erythema and ulceration in the descending and sigmoid colon, with normal-appearing mucosa in the ascending colon, transverse colon, and rectum. 

Biopsy specimens from the affected segments showed subepithelial edema, hemorrhage, mild crypt architectural distortion, and an acute inflammatory infiltrate without granulomas or dysplasia.

payload.vignette:
A 27-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of gross hematuria, right lower-quadrant pain, and low-grade fever. She had been treated empirically for presumed urinary tract infection with nitrofurantoin without relief; her hematuria recurred and flank pain worsened, prompting emergency evaluation.

On examination, her temperature was 38.8 °C. There was tenderness to palpation in the right upper and suprapubic regions. Urinalysis showed 2+ blood but no evidence of infection; urine β-hCG was negative. Laboratory studies revealed a normal white-cell count and mild anemia (hemoglobin, 11.2 g/dL; hematocrit, 33.2 %). Renal and hepatic function tests were normal.

A noncontrast abdominopelvic CT scan showed a large, heterogeneously attenuating right renal mass (approximately 10 cm) with foci of hyperattenuation suggesting hemorrhage and ipsilateral retroperitoneal edema; no nephrolithiasis or hydronephrosis was seen, and the left kidney was normal. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing expansile mass in the upper pole of the right kidney with invasion of the collecting system, right renal vein, and inferior vena cava. Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI confirmed a large right upper-pole renal mass with intralesional cystic change and hemorrhage, marked diffusion restriction, and tumoral extension into the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. A staging chest CT showed multiple small bilateral pulmonary nodules.

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was noted by his parents to have a slowly developing limitation in right-eye movement over several weeks. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including an infectious work-up, were negative.  
Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a well-circumscribed extraconal mass at the right superolateral orbital wall, adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture, with smooth bone remodeling and fluid-attenuating content but no bone invasion. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a cystic mass in the right superior extraconal compartment that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on FLAIR imaging, and exhibited no diffusion restriction or internal enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion exerted mild compression on the external and superior rectus muscles, correlating with the abduction deficit, but did not involve the optic nerve, intraconal fat, or show intracranial extension.

She had no prior evaluations and was referred for upper endoscopy, which revealed a large antral mass; a mucosal biopsy was obtained, but she declined endoscopic ultrasound and was lost to follow-up during pregnancy. She later returned with ongoing anemia and new epigastric pain. Repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound identified a 6 cm mass arising from the muscularis propria of the gastric antrum. Preoperative computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 9.7 × 7.8 × 4.8 cm heterogeneous mass adherent to the posterior wall of the gastric antrum, with predominantly fat attenuation, internal septations, and no pathologic lymphadenopathy. She then presented with melena; a repeat endoscopy showed mucosal ulceration overlying the mass, and biopsy results were consistent with adipose tissue.

payload.vignette:
A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of intermittent epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Her medical history was notable for poor mobility, type II diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. Eight years earlier, she had been admitted with Escherichia coli sepsis; an abdominal ultrasound at that time had incidentally shown a partially calcified gallbladder without signs of inflammation, and benign fatty changes in the liver. No intervention was pursued given her comorbidities.

On this admission, vital signs were within normal limits and general examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed no organomegaly or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed: ALT 45 U/L, ALP 775 U/L, total bilirubin 20 µmol/L, albumin 27 g/L, GGT 553 U/L, adjusted calcium 2.73 mmol/L, and a leukocyte count of 10.8×10^9/L.

payload.vignette:
A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

A 60-year-old Ugandan woman, recently diagnosed with HIV and not yet on antiretroviral therapy, was brought to the hospital with a one-day history of reduced consciousness, abrupt onset of aphasia, and urinary incontinence. She also reported a two-day history of dry cough, drenching night sweats, and weight loss but denied fever, headache, neck stiffness, visual disturbances, photophobia, or seizures.

On examination, she appeared wasted (weight 40 kg) and was afebrile (36.6 °C). Vital signs were: blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, pulse 66 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Neurologically, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14/15, with dysarthria but no other focal deficits; neck was supple, and pupils were equal and reactive. Chest and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Two days before admission, a non-contrast brain CT scan showed multiple enhancing nodular white matter lesions with significant peri-lesional edema and midline shift, as well as several small subcortical non-enhancing hypoattenuating lesions suggestive of infarcts. Initial laboratory testing revealed a CD4 count of 6 cells/mm^3 and a positive serum cryptococcal antigen test with a titer of 1:320. Lumbar puncture was deferred given the CT findings.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Therefore, the working diagnosis was a giant‐cell tumor of the tendon sheath. No further imaging was performed.

A 23-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to IgA nephropathy, maintained on peritoneal dialysis (four exchanges daily; he had missed his last two), was brought to a community hospital after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He reported headache and blurred vision for several hours prior. On arrival he was combative and confused, with blood pressure >182/107 mmHg; he received labetalol 20 mg IV, lorazepam 1 mg IV, and haloperidol 1 mg IV before transfer.

At the tertiary care center: temperature 36.8 °C; blood pressure 200/100 mmHg; heart rate 63 bpm; oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was rousable but confused, alert to person and place. Neurologic exam, including language and fundoscopy, was normal; there was no meningismus. Cardiovascular exam revealed a loud S2; respiratory and abdominal exams were unremarkable.

ECG demonstrated tall peaked T waves consistent with hyperkalemia. Noncontrast head CT revealed multiple cortical and subcortical hypodensities in the posterior parasagittal parietal lobes and the medial right occipital lobe, reported as suggestive of PRES.

A 42-year-old African American woman with a history of stage IIIB colon adenocarcinoma (post hemicolectomy and chemotherapy completed September 2020), paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, iron deficiency anemia, and lumbar radiculopathy presented in early March 2021 with a 2-week history of bilateral ear pain. The earache began on the right, then involved the left ear, radiating to the lateral and anterior neck and lower jaw bilaterally. It was worsened by head movement, swallowing, and coughing. She denied fever, fatigue, malaise, anorexia, myalgia, dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, cough, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, or ear discharge. She had no history of thyroid disease, head or neck radiation, or family history of head and neck cancer.

Exam: tender 3 cm anterior neck swelling.  
Labs: WBC 6.4×10³/µL; Hgb 13.2 g/dL; Plt 207×10³/µL; BUN 10 mg/dL; Cr 0.43 mg/dL; normal electrolytes and LFTs; TSH <0.0005 IU/mL (prior TSH 2.03 IU/mL one week before vaccination); total T3 1.90 ng/dL; free T4 1.51 ng/dL; ESR 81 mm/h; thyroid peroxidase antibodies <10 IU/mL.  
Thyroid ultrasound: right lobe heterogeneous mass 1.6×1.4×3.4 cm; left lobe hypoechoic, moderately heterogeneous mass 1.6×1.8×3.4 cm; no calcifications; mildly enlarged left paratracheal lymph nodes.
