payload.vignette:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

payload.vignette:
A 55-year-old right-handed man with no significant medical history presented with two days of worsening “heaviness” in his right arm. He denied gait difficulty, pain, sensory changes, or cranial symptoms. He had an upper respiratory illness three weeks earlier and denied diarrhea or recent vaccinations. On arrival, blood pressure was 220/139 mm Hg; he was afebrile and alert. Examination showed uniform weakness of the right upper extremity (motor strength 3/5) with 1+ reflexes; left upper extremity and bilateral lower extremities had strength 5/5 with 2+ reflexes. Sensation was intact, cranial nerves were normal, and he walked unassisted. Urine toxicology, head CT, brain MRI with diffusion‐weighted imaging, and cervical‐spine imaging were all unremarkable. He was admitted for observation. On hospital day 2, lumbar puncture showed 1 white blood cell, no red blood cells, and protein 33 mg/dL. Serum assay for botulinum toxin was negative. On hospital day 3, right arm strength declined to 2/5, and new left arm weakness (4/5) appeared; repeat MRI remained normal. On hospital day 4, he was unable to walk unassisted, had complete flaccid paralysis of the right arm, left arm strength 3/5, and areflexia throughout all extremities.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

payload.vignette:
A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

payload.vignette:
A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. At 22, she had trochanteric bursitis and an X-ray showed a Q-angle of 17°; no metabolic evaluation was done. She takes OTC vitamin D3 without calcium. She is 155 cm tall, weighs 58.5 kg (BMI 23.8), with no personal or family history of fractures or metabolic bone disease.

On exam, there is marked bilateral valgus alignment (left > right) with a knocking gait. Repeat X-ray shows a Q-angle of 23°. Bone density scanning reveals osteopenia of the left femoral head and normal lumbar spine density. Laboratory studies show:
• Serum phosphate: low  
• Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: elevated  
• Parathyroid hormone: low  
• FGF23: undetectable  

A 24-hour urine collection demonstrates inappropriately normal phosphate excretion for the degree of hypophosphatemia and normal urine calcium. Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis without stones.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

payload.vignette:
A 49-year-old woman was referred for surgical management of a presumed large nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma. She reported a 2-year history of chronic bitemporal headache, unexplained easy fatigability, and very slowly progressive diminution of vision. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, visual acuity was decreased bilaterally (worse on the left) with bitemporal homonymous hemianopia. Endocrinological evaluation revealed central hypothyroidism, and levothyroxine replacement was initiated. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a slightly hyperdense large sellar/suprasellar mass extending into both cavernous sinuses with right parasellar extension and bony remodeling of the sella turcica and upper clivus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 36 × 41 × 50 mm sellar/suprasellar/parasellar mass with heterogeneous low T1 signal, intermediate high T2 signal, small central areas of diffusion restriction on DWI, and mild patchy postcontrast enhancement. The lesion encased the cavernous and clinoid segments of the right internal carotid artery and partially encased the left cavernous segment. The optic nerves and chiasm were elevated and inseparable from the mass, and the pituitary gland and stalk were not visualized.

payload.vignette:
A 34-year-old woman presented with 6 months of progressive left proptosis, with recent ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage after a sudden rise in blood pressure. She had intact ocular motility, a best-corrected visual acuity of 0.9 in the left eye, and normal anterior and posterior segment examinations without optic nerve signs. The right eye was anophthalmic following enucleation in 2010 for a large choroidal melanoma confirmed by histopathology and metastatic workup; she received no adjuvant therapy and was lost to follow-up after 2 years of disease-free status. Orbital CT showed a well-defined isodense intraconal lesion measuring 2.6 × 2.5 × 2.4 mm with intrinsic high-density areas, located inferomedially between the optic nerve and inferior rectus, displacing them and scalloping the lamina papyracea. MRI demonstrated a hyperintense mass on T1-weighted images and hypointense signal on T2-weighted images. General physical examination and systemic metastatic evaluation were negative. An incisional biopsy via anterior inferomedial transconjunctival orbitotomy was planned.

payload.vignette:
A 66-year-old man was referred for recurrent perianal abscesses over 12 months. His history included perianal trauma from sitting on broken glass in childhood; comorbidities were vascular dementia, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and gout. He reported no perianal warts, sexually transmitted diseases, immune deficiency, inflammatory dermatoses, arsenic exposure, or family history of malignancy. Examination revealed a fluctuant left lateral perianal mass without external fistulas. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration yielded 15 cc of purulent fluid; Gram stain and cultures were negative, but cytology showed atypical squamous cells. Postdrainage differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma, cyst, condyloma, or large abscess. Two months later, the mass had enlarged, prompting concern for a fistula. Surgical drainage again yielded purulent fluid without microbial growth. On examination under anesthesia less than one month later, an external sinus tract into the mass was noted but no fistula to the anal canal. It was then decided to excise the mass completely and close the defect primarily.

payload.vignette:
An 18-year-old man presented with 20 days of pain and swelling around his right scapula, which had been gradually increasing in size, and 2 days of fever. He had been receiving anti-tubercular therapy for presumed pulmonary tuberculosis for 6 months; the diagnosis had been based on cough, chest radiograph findings, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with negative sputum studies. Despite continued therapy, 3 days before presentation he developed swelling and pain of the left ankle with difficulty walking. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/h and a positive C-reactive protein level of 96 mg/L. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder and left ankle demonstrated findings consistent with osteomyelitis involving the scapula and the distal tibia. An aspiration of the scapular swelling was performed, and specimens were sent for culture, sensitivity testing, and histopathologic examination for possible multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

payload.vignette:
An 86-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of skin lesions on his abdomen and lower back. He reported occasional blurry vision and joint aches but denied weight loss, chills, abdominal pain, bleeding, or healing problems. His medical history was notable only for a 20–pack-year smoking history (quit 50 years ago) and no history of skin cancer. On examination, there were numerous moderately severe, irregular, erythematous papules and nodules on the abdomen and lower back. Laboratory results from 1 month earlier showed leukopenia (white cells 1,900/μL), anemia (3.24 million RBC/μL), mild thrombocytopenia (128,000/μL), and neutropenia (766/μL). C-reactive protein was elevated at 19.5 mg/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 249 U/L. A panel for sexually transmitted infections was negative. A shave biopsy of a representative papule revealed in the dermis a dense infiltrate of monotonous neoplastic cells with dispersed chromatin and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.

payload.vignette:
A 56-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-week history of dry cough and mild weight loss. She denied fever, haemoptysis, night sweats, and had no known contacts with tuberculosis. Two courses of antibiotics produced no improvement. On examination, coarse crepitations were heard over the right upper and lower lung zones. A chest radiograph showed an air-space opacity in the right upper lobe. CT of the thorax demonstrated multifocal consolidations in the right upper lobe extending to the right lower lobe. Given the clinical and radiographic suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis, she was started empirically on anti-tuberculosis therapy. After 2 weeks, her symptoms persisted. A Mantoux tuberculin skin test showed 10 mm of induration. Sputum induction for acid-fast bacilli was negative, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Xpert® Mycobacterium tuberculosis/rifampicin assay as well as bacterial and fungal cultures. Hence, a CT-guided lung biopsy was planned.

payload.vignette:
A 78-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-year history of progressive gait disturbance characterized by imbalance, slow walking, and repeated falls, accompanied initially by a head tremor. One year after onset, she developed recent memory impairment and occasional psychotic episodes. Over the subsequent years, her walking disability worsened to a rigid-akinetic syndrome requiring support for ambulation, and she eventually became wheelchair-bound. Nonmotor symptoms included reduced speech output, impaired comprehension, emotional lability, and dependency in daily activities.  

On brain MRI performed in 2022, there was diffuse, generalized hyperintensity of the supratentorial white matter on T2/FLAIR sequences involving all cerebral lobes. No contrast enhancement was seen on T1 postgadolinium images, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no areas of restricted diffusion.  

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a mildly elevated protein concentration of 56.6 mg/dL (reference range, 15–45 mg/dL), with a normal cell count (0 cells/mm3) and glucose level (59 mg/dL). Tests for KOH, bacterioscopy, culture, cytology, and JC virus in the CSF were negative.

payload.vignette:
A 68-year-old retired man with no prior medical history presented with two months of dorsal spine pain and gradually progressive motor weakness of the left lower extremity. One week before admission, his weakness acutely worsened, rendering him unable to stand or walk without assistance; there was no history of trauma.  

On neurologic examination, he had spastic paraparesis with weakness of the quadriceps, hamstrings, ankle dorsiflexors, and toe extensors on the left. Patellar and ankle jerks were increased, with sustained clonus at the left ankle and bilateral Babinski signs. Superficial hypoesthesia was present below the T7 level, and bladder and bowel function were preserved.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervico-thoracic spine revealed a well-circumscribed, extra-axial mass posterolateral to the right side of the spinal cord at C7–T1, causing marked canal stenosis and cord deformation. The lesion was intermediate in signal intensity on T1-weighted images and homogeneously low in signal on T2-weighted images. On fat-saturated postcontrast T1-weighted images, it demonstrated a thin rim of enhancement with no internal enhancement.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging right breast swelling. She had no history of tuberculosis or tuberculous contact and no family history of cancer. Ultrasonography and mammography showed an ACR-4 lesion in the supero-external quadrant of the right breast, and empirical fluoroquinolone was started. After 7 days, a skin fistula developed with pus extruding and an “orange peel” appearance of the overlying skin. Breast MRI revealed multiple oval and rounded lesions with irregular thick walls throughout the gland, extending to the skin, with peripheral enhancement.

A 27-month-old girl was evaluated for progressive right periorbital swelling of three weeks’ duration without preceding trauma. Two weeks earlier, she had been treated with ophthalmic ointment and eye drops without improvement, and the eyelid became erythematous. An outside pediatrician diagnosed periorbital cellulitis and prescribed oral cefaclor for two weeks, but the swelling and redness persisted. Her medical history was unremarkable, and immunizations were up to date.

On transfer, laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 0.59 mg/dL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 57 mm/h; other test results were within normal limits. An orbital CT scan revealed a destructive lesion centered on the anterior wall of the right maxillary sinus, forming a large soft-tissue mass that protruded into the sinus; a small fluid-attenuated focus was noted in the anterior portion of the mass. On MRI, the lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images; within the cystic portion, a fluid-fluid level was identified. The mass demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration and invaded the ipsilateral inferior orbital wall and extraconal space. Adjacent soft-tissue edema and fat infiltration involved the right cheek and periorbital area. The maxillary alveolar processes and teeth were intact. Serial imaging over two weeks showed rapid enlargement of the mass.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Adjacent soft-tissue edema and fat infiltration involved the right cheek and periorbital area. The maxillary alveolar processes and teeth were intact. Serial imaging over two weeks showed rapid enlargement of the mass.

Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes mellitus, or vasculitis. On examination, vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated right profound sensorineural hearing loss. High-resolution CT of the temporal bones showed an irregularly enhancing mass in the right ear canal, middle ear cavity, and mastoid air cells, with erosive changes of the skull base and extension into the right middle cranial fossa.

payload.vignette:
An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

payload.vignette:
An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a facial angioma. MRI of the brain showed no leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Examination revealed bilateral naevus flammeus along the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, more extensive on the right. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Funduscopic examination showed increased retinal vessel tortuosity and a diffusely darker fundus in the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography measured choroidal thickness of 2.2 mm in the right eye versus 1.4 mm in the left. Macular spectral-domain OCT confirmed a thicker choroid in the right eye. Standard automated perimetry detected early visual-field defects in the right eye, and peripapillary OCT showed borderline retinal nerve-fibre-layer thickness on the right. Topical latanoprost was initiated in the right eye, reducing intraocular pressure to 17 mm Hg.

payload.vignette:
A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 57 bpm, first-degree AV block, and a prolonged QTc. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 45–50% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Telemetry captured intermittent high-grade AV block with ventricular escape beats, prompting placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker.

Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries, and left ventriculography showed an LVEF of 35–40%. A permanent dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted, and he was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure.

Outpatient cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 31%, RV ejection fraction of 23%, and mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal anteroseptal wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

Over two and a half years, he underwent extensive physiotherapy for presumed plantar fasciitis and tight gastrocnemius muscles, treatment with anti-inflammatory and analgesic medications, and two separate surgical releases (endoscopic plantar fascia release and minimally invasive gastrocnemius release) with only temporary relief. On re-presentation, he reported recurrent heel pain upon return to work.

On examination, he walked with an antalgic gait. The gastrocnemius remained tight with a positive Silfverskiöld test, and there was non-specific tenderness over the plantar aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the plantar fascia.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot showed no thickening of the plantar fascia and no signal alteration in adjacent soft tissues or bone marrow. However, MRI revealed a pedunculated bony protrusion arising from the posterolateral plantar aspect of the calcaneus, measuring approximately 1.1 cm × 0.9 cm.

payload.vignette:
A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 2 days of sharp, stabbing right-sided chest pain (8/10) worsened by exertion and relieved by leaning forward, accompanied by shortness of breath on minimal activity. She also reported chronic right lower-leg swelling and six months of symmetric wrist stiffness that improved during the day. Her history included heavy menstrual bleeding, a miscarriage at age 14, chronic warfarin-refractory deep vein thromboses, and placement of a nonretrievable inferior vena cava filter. She denied fevers, chills, or intravenous drug use.

On examination she was obese and mildly tachypneic, sitting forward. Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F, blood pressure 116/91 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had a malar rash, jugular venous distension, tender anterior chest wall, bibasilar Velcro crackles, and a grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increased with inspiration.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 71 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 55 mm/h, CRP 90.9 mg/L, D-dimer 3.7 µg/mL, and prolonged PTT of 49 s with normal PT/INR/fibrinogen. Blood cultures were negative. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated small bilateral pleural effusions and multifocal atelectasis without pulmonary embolism. Lower-extremity duplex ultrasound was negative for DVT. Chest radiograph revealed cardiomegaly, blunting of the right costophrenic angle, and elevated bilateral hemidiaphragms. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 55–60%, moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation, a 1.6 × 0.9 cm tricuspid-valve vegetation, and mild pericardial effusion. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed vegetations on all three tricuspid leaflets.

Based on these findings, rheumatic heart disease and nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis were considered in the differential diagnosis.

payload.vignette:
A 54-year-old woman was brought to the neurosurgical emergency department by her family because of a two-month history of progressive mental confusion with marked worsening over the past two weeks, leading to complete dependence for basic activities of daily living. Her only past medical history was well-controlled hypertension. She had grown up on a farm and had regular contact with various birds, including pigeons. 

On examination, she was normotensive and in poor general condition, able only to obey simple commands. Gait could not be assessed because she was bedbound due to generalized weakness. There were no focal motor deficits, no cranial-nerve abnormalities, and no meningeal signs. Her score on the Karnofsky performance scale was 50. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, performed a few days earlier, revealed two left occipital lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema. She had no other systemic abnormalities. Preoperative laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram, were all within normal limits. 

Given the radiographic appearance and the clinical decline, the decision was made to proceed with neurosurgical resection of the occipital lesions.

payload.vignette:
An 18-year-old woman presented with 2 days of fever and vomiting followed by 1 day of weakness in all four limbs and speech difficulty. Her temperature was 101.4 °F; other vital signs were normal. She was fully conscious (GCS 15). Fundoscopic examination was normal. Neurologically, she had bilateral horizontal gaze palsy with impaired oculocephalic reflexes, bulbar dysarthria, and quadriplegia with bilateral extensor plantar responses; there were no signs of meningeal irritation. Chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed anemia, reduced packed cell volume, and thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a normal total cell count (all lymphocytes) and mildly elevated protein. Serum dengue NS1 antigen was positive; anti-dengue IgM and IgG were not detected. MRI of the brain demonstrated T1 hypointensity and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the bilateral thalami, pons, medulla, and left cerebellum, with intense diffusion restriction on DWI and central blooming on GRE sequences, producing a “double-doughnut” appearance; there was also an acute infarct in right frontal white matter.

payload.vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned. She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation. She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy.

On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.” A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area. There were no signs of steroid-induced atrophy, such as skin thinning or increased vascular prominence.

payload.vignette:
A 35-year-old woman presented with a 15-month history of vaginal bleeding and intermittent sensation of a mass in the vagina. She described bleeding with clots every 1–2 weeks lasting 2–5 days without a separate menstrual cycle; between bleeding episodes she had a watery, nonfoul-smelling vaginal discharge and occasional postcoital bleeding. She denied dyspnea, palpitations, or bleeding from other sites. Her obstetric history included three home vaginal deliveries; she underwent minilaparotomy sterilization 11 years prior and tubal recanalization 5 years ago. Prior evaluations—including coagulation studies, pelvic ultrasonography, and empiric therapy with progesterone, tranexamic acid, and antibiotics—had not alleviated her symptoms.

On examination she appeared pale but hemodynamically stable. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. On bimanual pelvic examination there was a firm, globular 6×4 cm mass within the vaginal canal; a separate cervical os could not be identified and the uterine fundus was not palpable. Active vaginal bleeding was noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL with normal platelet count and PT/INR. Pelvic ultrasonography—performed multiple times, including in the preoperative area—was reported as normal and was unable to clarify the origin of the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available. After resuscitation with intravenous fluids and two units of whole blood, she was scheduled for emergency surgical management.

payload.vignette:
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

payload.vignette:
A 17-year-old boy presented on the fourth day of an acute febrile illness. He reported fever and severe myalgia for 4 days, productive cough with yellow sputum but no hemoptysis, and 3 days of watery diarrhea. On the day of transfer, he developed oliguria and noted red-colored urine. He denied trauma, exertion, medication ingestion, or freshwater exposures.

On examination, temperature 38.4 °C, pulse 102 bpm, blood pressure 100/80 mm Hg, GCS 15. He appeared unwell, with generalized muscle tenderness and restricted movement due to pain. Chest auscultation was clear bilaterally; the abdomen revealed right hypochondrial tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed reduced ionized calcium 8.16 mg/dL, elevated phosphate 5.4 mg/dL, and normal magnesium. Initial abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. He was admitted to the ICU and treated with acetaminophen and empiric intravenous cefotaxime and clarithromycin. Over the next ten hours he developed sinus tachycardia up to 150–195 bpm and hypotension requiring fluid adjustments guided by central venous pressure and vasopressors. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were unremarkable. A repeat abdominal ultrasound remained normal. Urinalysis showed no red cells, mild proteinuria, and 6–8 pus cells per high-power field. Serum creatine phosphokinase was markedly elevated at over 90,000 U/L.

payload.vignette:
A 21-year-old woman presented with lifelong uncorrectable visual acuity and color vision impairment. There was no consanguinity in her family. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. She had myopia (–6.0 diopters) and intraocular pressures of 17 mmHg bilaterally. Fundus examination showed slight enlargement of the cup-to-disc ratio in both eyes. Visual field testing revealed a central scotoma in both eyes. Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging demonstrated symmetric hypoautofluorescent lesions with hyperautofluorescent borders in the central macula bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed thinning of the outer nuclear layer in the fovea, partial preservation of the ellipsoid zone, and a normal retinal nerve fiber layer. Full-field electroretinography (ff-ERG) revealed normal scotopic responses but attenuated photopic responses and 30-Hz flicker responses with delayed implicit times in both eyes.

Her 54-year-old father reported over 10 years of progressive blurred central vision and color vision defects. He had myopia (–3.0 diopters) and no other relevant family history. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed macular atrophy and lesions bilaterally. FAF imaging showed an outer ring of increased autofluorescence with central hypoautofluorescence in the macula of both eyes. OCT demonstrated loss of the ellipsoid zone and collapse of the outer nuclear layer in the central macula bilaterally. ff-ERG showed delayed implicit times in the dark-adapted 0.01 ERG, an electronegative waveform in the dark-adapted 3.0 ERG, and non-recordable photopic and 30-Hz flicker responses in both eyes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

OCT demonstrated loss of the ellipsoid zone and collapse of the outer nuclear layer in the central macula bilaterally. ff-ERG showed delayed implicit times in the dark-adapted 0.01 ERG, an electronegative waveform in the dark-adapted 3.0 ERG, and non-recordable photopic and 30-Hz flicker responses in both eyes.

payload.vignette:
A 1-year-old girl was brought with sudden onset of hematemesis; the vomitus resembled coffee grounds. She was born full-term, had no significant medical or family history, no allergies, and no medication use, including NSAIDs. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 9,500/μL; hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL; platelets 220×10^3/μL; CRP 0.55 mg/dL; normal liver function tests; prothrombin time 13.2 s (INR 1.01); aPTT 31.7 s; normal factor XIII and plasma gastrin levels; ESR 2 mm/h. Abdominal radiography and ultrasonography were normal, and contrast-enhanced CT showed no active bleeding. She received two units of packed red blood cells and famotidine, yet her hemoglobin remained low. Thus, on hospital day 2, early upper endoscopy was planned to identify the bleeding source.

payload.vignette:
A 62-year-old man was admitted on June 25, 2021, with a 20-day history of episodic slurred speech that had worsened over the previous 9 days. Initially, episodes lasted about 10 minutes without loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, or limb weakness; by presentation, they occurred 2–3 times daily lasting about 30 minutes. His medical history included hypertension (>20 years), diabetes mellitus (8 years), and coronary heart disease (8 years); he was blind bilaterally after retinal detachment in adolescence. He denied smoking and alcohol use. On examination, temperature was 36.5°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and blood pressure 144/86 mmHg. Cranial nerve exam showed dysarthria and midline tongue extension; limb strength was 5/5 with normal tone; Babinski and other reflexes were normal; he had no light perception with irregular pupils and absent light reflexes. Routine blood tests, coagulation studies, rheumatologic panels, thyroid function, tumor markers, liver and kidney function, and electrolytes were all normal. Brain MRI and susceptibility-weighted imaging were unremarkable; MRA showed mild cerebral arteriosclerosis; carotid MRA showed carotid arteriosclerosis with limited stenosis of the intracranial left vertebral artery; transcranial Doppler was normal. The initial diagnosis was transient ischemic attack of the vertebrobasilar system. On review, symptoms did not improve with rest; a fatigue test and a neostigmine test were both negative.

payload.vignette:
A 48-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with a 3-month history of brown-yellowish vaginal discharge, fluctuating lower abdominal pain, fever, and progressive abdominal enlargement over 15 years, worsening in the last 5 years. She reported difficulty with defecation and voiding. She had undergone an attempted myomectomy in the past, but removal was aborted due to severe adhesions. There was no relevant drug or family history.

On rectovaginal examination, a smooth, firm pelvic mass was palpated extending to two fingers below the umbilicus, with limited mobility; the cervix could not be visualized or sondaged. Laboratory studies showed an elevated Cancer Antigen 125 level of 115.6 g/dL.

Transabdominal ultrasound revealed a 269 × 529 mm hypoechoic mass within the uterine cavity, suspected to represent infected hematometra, and a separate 126 × 106 mm homogeneous solid mass in the left adnexa with a clear border, raising suspicion for an intraligamentary myoma with cystic degeneration or a left ovarian fibroid.

Abdominal and pelvic computed tomography demonstrated a 145 × 110 × 146 mm multilocular cystic mass with thick septa and enhancing solid components, clearly demarcated from the uterus and bladder, displacing the uterus to the right superior-lateral side. The uterine cavity was distended with fluid and air forming an air-fluid level. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

payload.vignette:
A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

payload.vignette:
A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

payload.vignette:
A 50-year-old man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas, and no history of smoking, was admitted for recurrent urinary retention and sepsis. A transurethral resection of the prostate revealed fibroleiomyomatous hyperplasia, but urinary function did not improve. Laboratory studies and a CT scan showed diffuse irregular polypoid thickening of the entire bladder wall without a discrete mass. Because of compromised bladder function, the patient underwent cystoprostatectomy. 

On gross examination, the bladder wall was diffusely thickened, firm, and gray–white, with near–complete loss of the detrusor muscle. Histologic evaluation revealed in the superficial wall a diffuse bland spindle cell proliferation with comma-shaped nuclei and a collagenous matrix. In the deeper wall, there was a dense, perivascular spindle cell proliferation with prominent cytological atypia, frequent mitoses, and an infiltrative growth pattern. The tumor was in close contact with peripheral nerves. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for S100, p16, neurofilaments, and CD56, and negative for pan-cytokeratin, EMA, MDM2, p63, ALK, CD117, DOG1, myogenin, desmin, and smooth muscle actin.

A 50-year-old man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas, and no history of smoking, was admitted for recurrent urinary retention and sepsis. A transurethral resection of the prostate revealed fibroleiomyomatous hyperplasia, but urinary function did not improve. Laboratory studies and a CT scan showed diffuse irregular polypoid thickening of the entire bladder wall without a discrete mass. Because of compromised bladder function, the patient underwent cystoprostatectomy. 

On gross examination, the bladder wall was diffusely thickened, firm, and gray–white, with near–complete loss of the detrusor muscle. Histologic evaluation revealed in the superficial wall a diffuse bland spindle cell proliferation with comma-shaped nuclei and a collagenous matrix. In the deeper wall, there was a dense, perivascular spindle cell proliferation with prominent cytological atypia, frequent mitoses, and an infiltrative growth pattern. The tumor was in close contact with peripheral nerves. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for S100, p16, neurofilaments, and CD56, and negative for pan-cytokeratin, EMA, MDM2, p63, ALK, CD117, DOG1, myogenin, desmin, and smooth muscle actin.

payload.vignette:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

payload.vignette:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

payload.vignette:
A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.

He had a history of HBV-positive hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with partial hepatectomy, entecavir, transarterial chemoembolization, sorafenib, regorafenib, and pembrolizumab over the preceding two years. Physical examination revealed an ~8×4 cm subcutaneous mass over the right hypochondriac and flank regions; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Abdominal CT showed multiple nodules in liver segments 5 and 7 (largest 3.5 cm) and a right-flank soft tissue mass invading the 12th rib measuring 8×4×4 cm. Based on the clinical history and imaging, extrahepatic metastasis of HCC was suspected, but a primary soft tissue sarcoma could not be excluded. After discussion, surgical excision of the flank mass was performed without complications.

payload.vignette:
A 41-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening fever, weight loss, night sweats, and a dry cough. He also reported chronic lower back pain without neurologic deficits and a painful nonhealing ulcer on his right hallux. He had two sputum GeneXpert tests at local clinics, both negative. He was treated symptomatically with paracetamol, NSAIDs, and topical antibacterials.  

On referral for the toe ulcer, examination revealed a cachectic man who was normotensive and afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy or edema. He had tenderness over the thoracic spine but no neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests showed:  
• Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white cells 7.3×10^9/L, platelets 369×10^9/L  
• ESR >130 mm/hr, CRP 113 mg/L  
• IgA 6.2 g/L, anti-DNase B 259 IU/mL  
• Negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis serologies  
• Urine protein-creatinine ratio 0.242 g/mmol; dipstick: 3+ leukocytes, 3+ red blood cells; microscopy: granular casts; urine culture: no growth  

Chest radiograph showed bilateral reticular-nodular opacities. An induced sputum was trace positive for MTB on GeneXpert and subsequently grew MTB sensitive to rifampicin and isoniazid. Biopsy of the toe ulcer showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with a solitary acid-fast bacillus. MRI of the spine revealed contiguous spondylitis from T6 to T10 with discitis and an epidural/paraspinal collection causing spinal cord compression. Renal ultrasound demonstrated normal-sized kidneys with increased echogenicity.

The final histopathology showed granulomatous inflammation with central necrobiosis, extensive Alcian-Blue positive mucin, and scattered multinucleated giant cells. payload.vignette:
A 40-year-old previously healthy man was admitted after 1 week of progressive apathy, unresponsiveness, and immobility. He became bedridden and required a feeding tube and urinary catheter. On transfer, he was in a vegetative state.  
Vital signs: temperature 36.5 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 135/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E3 V1 M3). Pupils 3.5 mm, briskly reactive; corneal reflexes present. Both axial and appendicular muscles were rigid, with flexed arms and extended legs; bilateral Babinski and Chaddock signs were positive.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 3.79×10^9/L, neutrophils 74%, CRP 6.07 mg/L, ESR 21 mm/h; HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ANA, anticardiolipin, ANCA, and T-spot negative. Liver and renal functions were normal.  
Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 50 mmH₂O; CSF clear, protein 3.64 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (blood glucose 5.38 mmol/L), chloride 123 mmol/L, leukocytes 0/mm³. CSF India ink stain and bacterial cultures were negative. CSF oligoclonal bands, AQP4, MOG, and GFAP antibodies were negative; CSF fungal cultures were negative.  
Imaging: Brain CT showed a hypodense lesion in the corpus callosum. MRI revealed a homogeneous mass in the corpus callosum body, hypointense on T1, isointense on T2 FLAIR, with rim enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema on postcontrast T1. DWI demonstrated rim hyperintensity but no central restricted diffusion.

payload.vignette:
A 68-year-old man with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy underwent Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) in the right eye. His postoperative course was initially uneventful under topical and systemic corticosteroids. He had a history of an eye infection by Thaumetopoea pityocampa (pine processionary) 9 months before DSAEK, which had resolved prior to surgery.

Two months after DSAEK, he was referred for evaluation of keratitis in the right eye. On examination:
• Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.  
• Pupils were isocoric and isoreactive without an afferent pupillary defect.  
• There was no pain with ocular movements.  
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of the right eye showed brown, multilobular lesions confined to the deep corneal stroma, with no conjunctival hyperemia, no discharge, and no epithelial defect.  
• The anterior chamber was deep and clear. Intraocular pressure and fundus examination were normal. The left eye was unremarkable.

Anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the right eye revealed a central infiltrate involving all corneal layers and a peripheral infiltrate concentrated in the deep stroma.

payload.vignette:
A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

payload.vignette:
A 73-year-old man was treated for pneumonia when routine chest imaging revealed an incidental mass in the right posterior mediastinum. He had no compressive symptoms or systemic complaints. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hematocrit 25.7% (normal 38–52%), hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL (normal 13–18 g/dL), red-cell count 3.84 × 10^6/mm^3 (normal 4.0–5.5 × 10^6/mm^3), platelet count 88,000/mm^3 (normal 160,000–410,000/mm^3), and white-cell count 7000/mm^3 (normal 3800–8500/mm^3) with 58.3% neutrophils, 9.0% lymphocytes, and 25% eosinophils (normal 0–7%). A bone marrow smear revealed dysplastic megakaryocytes and erythrocytes without an increased number of blast cells, consistent with refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed a 38-mm oval, well-encapsulated mass in the posterior mediastinum. On MRI, the lesion had moderate signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. Because the radiographic findings were not typical for neurogenic tumors, the mass was surgically removed.

There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, the middle finger was enlarged but the overlying skin was normal. There was tenderness throughout the enlargement, the temperature was normal, and sensation was decreased distally. Resistance to flexion prevented full finger flexion. payload.vignette:
A 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer and a known left upper lobe lung mass presented with four weeks of progressive vertigo, described as the sensation that “the floor was wobbling” and “the room was swaying,” leading to difficulty ambulating. A few days before admission, he developed severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting. Two days prior, he was evaluated at an outside emergency department, tested positive for adenovirus, and was discharged after supportive treatment without symptom relief.

His oncology history included stage III prostate adenocarcinoma treated with prostatectomy and radiation in 2013, followed by detection of bilateral lung nodules and sclerotic bone lesions in 2016, and a 2020 biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirming mismatch repair deficient, androgen receptor–positive metastatic prostate cancer treated with enzalutamide, then abiraterone acetate and prednisone, and palliative radiation.

On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 164/81 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed no focal motor or sensory deficits; intact coordination on dysdiadochokinesia, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin testing; an intact gait despite dizziness; and a positive right-sided Dix–Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus.

Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema causing mild partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and left quadrigeminal cistern. The patient received dexamethasone. MRI of the brain demonstrated a cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect; no other intra-axial lesions were identified. Cerebral angiography revealed no abnormal hyperemia at the site of the lesion.

A hemangioblastoma was considered the leading diagnosis; other considerations included metastases and infarction.

payload.vignette:
A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability was brought to the hospital after a witnessed collapse. She had no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease, and her family denied any illicit drug or alcohol use. While at a noisy auto mechanic shop, she became pale and lost consciousness; bystander ECG showed ventricular fibrillation. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after two defibrillations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 93/70 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, and oxygen saturation 100% (bag–valve–mask). An intravenous amiodarone infusion (1 mg/min) and oral amiodarone 400 mg were administered. On examination she was comatose (GCS 3), with agonal respirations; cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. In the intensive care unit, her differential diagnosis included channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and metabolic abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed normal chemistry panel and electrolytes. Initial electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms, without any evidence of infarction, pre-excitation, or Brugada pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities.

payload.vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

payload.vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of burning sensation and discomfort in her left breast without fever or systemic symptoms. Escitalopram was discontinued and duloxetine increased to 100 mg/d while clonazepam was reduced. One week later, the paraesthesias persisted despite reducing duloxetine to 90 mg/d and clonazepam to 0.5 mg/d.

payload.vignette:
A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

On admission for a 2‐week educational trial of a plant‐based diet, his body weight was 69 kg and physical examination was unremarkable. Contrast‐enhanced CT and MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated swelling of the pancreas with a peripheral rim and slight narrowing of the main pancreatic duct. payload.vignette:
A 54-year-old African American woman with poorly controlled hypertension, a 15 pack-year smoking history, and alpha-thalassemia anemia presented after 3 weeks of progressive blurred vision, fatigue, headache, and orthopnea. She was referred for hypertensive retinopathy evaluation, where her blood pressure measured 220/130 mmHg and she had cotton-wool spots on funduscopic exam. In the emergency department, her systolic pressure reached 230 mmHg. On examination, jugular venous pressure was 14 cm above the sternal angle; heart sounds were distant without pulsus paradoxus; lungs were clear; and there was no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 11 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm/hr. Chest radiography demonstrated a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette with mild pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion (2.24 cm) with early right ventricular diastolic collapse, respirophasic mitral inflow variation, and a dilated inferior vena cava. payload.vignette:
A 74-year-old Spanish-speaking man visiting the United States from Honduras presented with a 2-month history of postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, night sweats, early satiety, and a 10-kg weight loss. One week earlier, an abdominal and pelvic CT scan had shown distal ileitis, and he had received a course of antibiotics without improvement. On re-presentation, he reported worsening symptoms and difficulty tolerating oral intake. He denied hematochezia, diarrhea, or fevers. His medical history was notable for prior appendectomy and recently treated helminth infection.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses, and no evidence of perianal disease. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 35 mg/L, and a fecal calprotectin of 94 μg/mg. Stool studies were negative for enteric pathogens. Repeat CT imaging demonstrated persistent distal ileitis.

Ileocolonoscopy revealed a normal terminal ileum, but a nontraversable distal ileal stricture, cecal ulcers, and patchy loss of vascularity throughout the colon. Segmental biopsies of the ileum and colon were obtained. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was positive. Hepatitis B serologies showed a reactive core total antibody, a reactive e antigen, negative surface antigen, and undetectable HBV DNA. He was started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis.

payload.vignette:
A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. Postoperatively, he was found to have HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 191 000 copies/mL. Serum toxoplasma IgG was elevated, and CSF studies showed 48 cells/µL (97% lymphocytes) with positive toxoplasma IgG and DNA-PCR for Toxoplasma gondii (286 copies/mL). Other CSF studies, including fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and AFB smear/culture, were negative. Histopathologic examination of the brain tissue revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites. He was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and started on antiretroviral therapy; empiric antibiotics for bacterial abscess were discontinued.

Two weeks after discharge, he returned with fever to 39.6 °C, generalized weakness, and a 1-day history of productive cough. Chest radiograph showed a new left upper lobe opacification with diffuse reticulonodular interstitial prominence. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions. His respiratory status worsened, and intubation was planned pending further diagnostic evaluation.
